content: Essential fatty acids (EFAs) are specific types of fatty acids that cannot be synthesized by the human body through any known biochemical pathways. As a result, they must be obtained through dietary intake. These fatty acids are critical for biological processes and are not merely used as an energy source. EFAs are categorized into two main families: omega-3 (ω-3 or n-3) and omega-6 (ω-6 or n-6). Both families are essential because the human body can interconvert fatty acids within the same family (e.g., one omega-3 to another omega-3) but cannot synthesize them de novo. Historically, EFAs were initially classified as Vitamin F when their essentiality was discovered in 1923. However, subsequent research in 1930 by Burr, Burr, and Miller demonstrated that they are better classified as fats rather than vitamins. In the human body, EFAs serve multiple critical functions. They are precursors for the synthesis of various bioactive compounds, including classic eicosanoids (which regulate inflammation and other cellular functions), endocannabinoids (which influence mood, behavior, and inflammation), lipoxins (derived from omega-6 EFAs), and resolvins (derived from omega-3 EFAs in the presence of aspirin, which help downregulate inflammation). Other derivatives include isofurans, neurofurans, isoprostanes, hepoxilins, epoxy-eicosatrienoic acids (EETs), and neuroprotectin D. EFAs also play a role in forming lipid rafts, which are essential for cellular signaling, and they can modulate gene expression by activating or inhibiting transcription factors such as NF-κB, which is associated with the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Fatty acids are straight-chain hydrocarbons with a carboxyl group (-COOH) at one end. The carbon atoms are labeled sequentially, with the one adjacent to the carboxyl group designated as α, the next as β, and so on. The terminal carbon is labeled as ω (omega). The position of the first double bond relative to the ω-carbon determines the classification of unsaturated fatty acids, such as ω-3 or ω-6. For example, an ω-3 fatty acid has its first double bond at the third carbon from the terminal methyl (CH3) end. The notation also includes the total number of carbons and double bonds, such as 18:4 ω-3, which indicates an 18-carbon chain with four double bonds and the first double bond at the third position from the ω-end. The two primary EFAs are alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, 18:3, ω-3) and linoleic acid (LA, 18:2, ω-6). Humans cannot synthesize these fatty acids due to the absence of the necessary desaturase enzymes. These short-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (SC-PUFAs) serve as precursors for the synthesis of longer and more unsaturated fatty acids, known as long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs). Examples of LC-PUFAs include eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, 20:5, ω-3), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6, ω-3), gamma-linolenic acid (GLA, 18:3, ω-6), dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3, ω-6), and arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4, ω-6). Omega-9 fatty acids, in contrast, are not essential because humans possess the enzymes required for their synthesis. The term essential in the context of fatty acids has evolved over time. Initially, arachidonic acid and linoleic acid were deemed essential based on their ability to support growth in rats fed fat-free diets. Later research confirmed that both ω-3 and ω-6 fatty acids are required for human metabolism. While any ω-3 or ω-6 fatty acid can alleviate the most severe symptoms of fatty acid deficiency, the specific balance and types of these fatty acids are crucial for optimal health. Some researchers argue that the dietary requirement for EFAs may be minimal if other dietary factors are optimized. EFAs are distinct from essential oils, which are concentrated plant extracts and are essential in the sense of containing the essence of the plant's fragrance or flavor. Dietary sources of EFAs include fish, shellfish, flaxseed, hemp oil, soybean oil, canola oil, chia seeds, pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds, leafy vegetables, and walnuts. Most of the polyunsaturated fats in the human diet are derived from EFAs. However, plant sources of ω-3 fatty acids do not contain EPA or DHA, which may explain why the absorption and utilization of EFAs are generally higher from animal sources than from plant sources. The fatty acid composition of animal-derived fats can vary significantly depending on the animal's diet and the specific body part from which the fat is obtained. EFAs play a vital role in numerous metabolic processes and are implicated in the maintenance of cardiovascular health. They are particularly important in the regulation of inflammation, cellular signaling, and gene expression. Deficiencies or imbalances in EFAs have been associated with various health conditions, underscoring their importance in human nutrition.
